intro:
Training went through four stages. Watch the videos in order and keep an eye on the Mean episode length and Linear velocity tracking reward charts.

1. Flailing (0–25). Random actions; the robot falls in about 1.7 s. 2. Giving up (25–100). Episodes get shorter. Every step costs a little penalty and the robot can't earn the walking reward yet, so ending the episode fast is the best deal on offer: the policy learns to fall on purpose. 3. Standing still (150–550). Once the upright and pose rewards outweigh the penalties, survival pays. The policy finds the safest way to collect them: stand and ignore the commands. 4. Walking (550+). Episodes jump to the 20 s limit in about 60 iterations (orange band). Only after that does the velocity tracking reward climb, and later iterations spend most of their effort on accuracy and smoothness.
0: Random network, exploration off. It never walks and topples about every 1.7 s, then respawns (11 falls). The 12 m 'distance' is mostly falling and stumbling, not walking.
50: The 'give up' phase: 125 falls in 20 s, roughly one every 8 steps. This is a policy that learned that ending the episode immediately loses the least reward. Compare the episode length chart, which drops to about 8 at this iteration.
150: It has started to value staying up. It survives about 1.7 s at a time and has learned some balance reflexes, but there's no stepping yet.
250: Zero falls for the first time. It stands still for the whole 20 s and ignores every command (0.4 m traveled). This is a local optimum: the upright and pose rewards are easy, and walking is risky.
400: Still standing still and still not falling. Training reward is flat here. It is slowly building the stability needed to move, but nothing shows on the course yet.
550: Inside the breakthrough band. Still mostly standing on this course (0.9 m), though some of the 4096 training robots are starting to survive full episodes.
600: Training robots now survive about 94% of the time limit, yet this one still stands. Survival came first; following the command comes next.
800: Walking. It follows forward, turn and sideways commands (5.8 m traveled), with speed error down to 0.19 m/s. The gait is cautious and the turns lag.
1500: Tracks the course well (speed error 0.11 m/s). Since 800, the gains have come from accuracy and smoothness, not from new skills.
2999: Final policy: speed error 0.10 m/s, turn error 0.06 rad/s, 7.6 m of the ideal 8.7 m. Almost everything after about 1500 iterations is polish.
